speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and ask him whether final disposition has been made of the question of forwarding a petition from the Indians to Her Majesty the Queen. Does the minister intend to follow the course previously outlined of looking into it himself rather than following the traditional policy toward Indians of permitting them to appeal direct to Her Majesty? If that is his view, will he table the petition so that we may know exactly the nature of this petition on behalf of these wards of the Canadian people who, while they have no votes, have rights?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having looked at Hansard for the past few days I rather anticipated I would be asked a question about this subject this morning. As I told the house on a previous occasion, since this petition came into my hands I have sought the advice of the legal advisers of the government as to the appropriate disposition to be made of it.
As hon. members are aware, and if they were not aware they were told I believe the day before yesterday by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the Queen in Canadian, affairs has only one group of advisers, her Canadian advisers. It is obvious that the Queen as a constitutional monarch can act only on advice. Obviously there would be no purpose served from any point of view by forwarding the petition without some responsibility being taken for such advice.
I have been advised by the deputy minister of justice and I shall read the advice I received from him as the house is perfectly entitled to know what I have received. This advice came to me in the usual constitutional 82715-70
manner through my deputy minister. The document is addressed to the deputy minister and reads as follows:
February 4, 1957.
The Deputy Minister,
Department of Citizenship and Immigration,
Woods Building,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,
I understand that Mrs. Gorman, barrister, of Calgary, sent a petition addressed to Her Majesty to His Excellency the Governor General concerning proposed amendments to the Indian Act and that His Excellency in turn referred the matter to you.
You have asked my opinion whether the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is required to take any action in respect of the matters petitioned for. In my opinion, he is not.
I might add that it is established practice for the Governor General to refer matters of this kind to the responsible minister.	.
Yours truly,
F. P. Varcoe,
Deputy Attorney General of Canada.
I may say that I have examined the petition and it does not appear to me to be in the form prescribed by the rules of the house for submission to the house. Since I am not an expert in these matters I would not wish to express any view of my own, but it does not appear to me that I should offer to table this petition without its being examined in the way prescribed by the rules. I may say, before the Leader of the Opposition gets too excited, that I would not have the slightest objection to the petition being made public; indeed I would be most happy that its contents should be known to every hon. member and to every other person interested, because the petition merely sets out the same arguments as have been made previously in other documents addressed to me and to the officers of my department. There is nothing new in it and there is no difference in substance from those arguments which have been made up to now by Mrs. Gorman, a barrister in Calgary, on behalf of the Indian Association of Alberta.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does the minister now say that the reason he will not table it is that this petition is not a petition that would be accepted by parliament if it had been made to parliament? Is that the ground?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
What I said, sir, was that I have looked up the rules and it did not appear to me that this petition was in the

Inquiries of the Ministry form prescribed by parliament, and that I would not venture to offer to table it without that point being considered by you, Mr. Speaker, or by the appropriate officers of the house.
As to the substance of it, I have not the slightest objection. I would certainly be delighted to make copies of it available to every hon. member. But I do not want to break the rules of the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. My point of order arises out of the statement which has just been made by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. He said the petition should be looked at, and its propriety determined, before he tables it. Is it not the practice according to our rules -and I am looking at standing order No. 70-for a member who has received a petition to table it, and for the decision as to whether or not the petition is in proper form to be made by the clerk of petitions?
Standing order No. 70 provides under paragraph (1) for a petition to be tabled. Without reading all the paragraphs I will proceed to paragraph (7) which states:
On the next day following the presentation of a petition the clerk of the house shall lay upon the table the report of the clerk of petitions upon the petitions presented and such report shall be printed m the Votes and Proceedings of that day.
And so on. I do not think the rest of it is relevant.
My point, Mr. Speaker, is that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is usurping a function of the clerk of the house and the clerk of petitions. The petition may well be in a form which is not proper, but should not the clerk of petitions make that decision rather than the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to the point of order which has been raised.
This is just another example of the minister taking upon himself, and arrogating to himself, a power of censorship which he does not possess. This is not a petition to parliament. This was a petition to Her Majesty the Queen, and the hon. gentleman, in what appears to me to be a monstrous perversion of his rights, refuses to permit that petition to go to its destination.
Then, when a proper request is made that parliament should at least know what is in the petition, the minister resorts to what I consider to be another subterfuge in order to deny Indians the opportunity of bringing their petition of wrongs before the house. I think Your Honour will agree that the state-
rnent made by the minister at this time, and his latest stand on this subject, show not only lack of knowledge of the rules but a continued desire to act tyrannously toward these Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: On the point just raised by the hon. gentleman, may I say that I did not refuse to table this petition, and I am not refusing to do so. I said that I wished to stay within the rules of the house, and that I needed guidance on that point.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is no doubt about that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
With regard to this matter of order which has been raised: In the first place one would have to know to whom the petition has been addressed, because it must be borne in mind, according to citation 584 of Beauchesne, third edition, that a member cannot be compelled to present a petition. And according to citation 593:
Every petition should commence with the superscription: "To the Honourable the House of Commons in Parliament assembled." Then should follow the formula:	"The Petition of the undersigned . . . humbly sheweth." Follows the subject-matter on the petition, in the third person through, and commencing each paragraph with the word "That". The conclusion should be the "Prayer" tersely and clearly expressing the particular object which the petitioners have in view in coming before parliament. The petition should close with the formal words: "and your petitioners, as in duty bound, will ever pray". Here follow the signatures which must be in writing and not typewritten or printed.
Without a prayer, a document will not be taken as a petition: and a paper, assuming the style of a declaration, an address of thanks, or a remonstrance only, without a proper form of prayer, will not be received.
There is no doubt that, according to standing order 70, once a petition is presented by a member, either by passing it over to the clerk or presenting it in the house at the beginning of routine proceedings, the clerk of petitions has the responsibility of examining it and making a report and the Speaker on that report will make a ruling whether or not the petition will be received. But it is up to the member who is in possession of the petition to do what he wishes, and that is the information which I think I might give the minister with respect to the matter. He is not compelled to deposit the petition, as it is said in citation 584, but if he wishes to do so he can leave it with the Clerk, the clerk of petitions will examine it and if it is not in conformity with the requirements of citation 593 the petition will have to be ruled out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: I thank Your Honour for this guidance and I will be glad to give the petition to the Clerk at the earliest possible moment.

I wish to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Since the minister has made himself the final addressee of the petition from the Indian Association of Alberta instead of sending it on to Her Majesty the Queen to whom it was addressed-
Question.
-has the minister sent a reply in answer to the petition to the Indian Association of Alberta? If so, what is the reply?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might begin by saying that it does not surprise me that several members of the Tory party seem to want to go back to the days before responsible government when this country was ruled from London.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is just nonsense.
We do not have responsible government at this time, so perhaps we ought to go back.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Our position on this side of the house is that it is our duty to take our constitutional responsibilities. Now that I have received the advice I sought from the law officer of the government, I intend to make a reply to the lady who submitted the petition.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand the hon. member for Wetaskiwin wishes to ask a supplementary question.

I should like to ask the minister if he would, as he indicated a few minutes ago, have copies of the petition made for individual members and send them to them, provided the form of the petition is such that it cannot be tabled in the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: I shall be glad to do that. [Later:']

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with reference to the letter from the deputy minister of justice which he read a few minutes ago, would the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration state whether he read the entire contents of that letter?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

Smart fellow.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Finance. Will the minister comment on the fact that at the moment when the Bank of England has reduced its rate from 5i per cent to 5 per cent the Bank of Canada rate has actually gone up from 3.95 per cent to 3.97 per cent?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO INCREASE IN DISCOUNT RATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the only comment that need be made is that the Bank of England raised its discount rate perhaps a year ago or a little more to what was considered to be an extraordinarily high rate and that this action was intended as a very pointed comment on the money market in the United Kingdom. The Bank of Canada have not felt it necessary to do that in Canada, though they did raise their rates successively during the last year when, I think, the rate reached 3J per cent by action of the Bank of Canada. Then a decision was made by the bank to establish the rate at J per cent above the going rate for 91-day treasury bills from week to week. The action of the Bank of England, as explained yesterday in the House of Commons at Westminster by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, has been anticipated for several months because of the improved position of sterling and the improved position generally of the United Kingdom with respect to its balance of payments problems and is nothing more than an indication- perhaps I should not interpret anything that the chancellor interpreted-that the problem which arose in the United Kingdom some months before it arose here has been dealt with successfully up to the present time by the same kind of action that is being adopted in Canada.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO INCREASE IN DISCOUNT RATE
speechtext: From what the minister has said am I to take it that we may quite well expect bur rates still to be going up?

We in Canada are now perhaps in the position that they were in six months to nine months ago.

speechtext:
I think I owe an explanation to the house with respect to the matter which I suggested be left in abeyance yesterday. We now have Hansard of yesterday and I am

Inquiries of the Ministry referring to page 1049. A question was asked by the hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska (Mr. Van Horne) which reads:
In view of the minister's answer yesterday, which I could not understand because of the covering-up noises of the Liberals, to the effect that he did not know of the several weeks' delay occurring in the processing of thousands of unemployment insurance claims, will the minister tell us when he will get busy and do his job and remove the dagger held over the backs of the workingmen of Canada? The minister's do-nothing attitude is that of a saboteur of the rights of the workingmen of Canada, and I am not going to stand for it.
At that moment I asked the hon. member to revise his language and he did not consider that he should be called upon to do so. A point of order was raised by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and at that point I said:
I would not want to have a discussion started on the exact words that have been used. I suggest that the matter be left in abeyance until I have had a chance to look at the transcript.
I have examined four dictionaries and have looked at the various definitions of the word that was used. In most instances the word "sabotage" is defined as the act of one who wants to damage or wreck. The King's English dictionary defines the expression as meaning malicious destruction of property. The expression is not one which I believe should be used, but I realize the consequences that may ensue should the Speaker ask that a certain expression be withdrawn. It may be that the sense of the house will not be behind his request or the hon. gentleman who has uttered the expression may not be disposed to adhere to the request of the Speaker. In such case it is automatic that the hon. member be named and then would follow all the consequences the house knows about.
I had hoped yesterday that the hon. member of his own volition would have done something about it and there is still time for him to do something if he so chooses. However, I am not going to insist upon the withdrawal of the word that has been used. For the benefit of hon. members I should like to read citation 234 of Beauchesne's third edition which is as follows:
It is impossible to lay down any specific rules, in regard to injurious reflections uttered in debate against particular members, or to declare beforehand, what expressions are or are not contrary to order: much depends upon the tone and manner, and intention, of the person speaking; sometimes upon the person to whom the words are addressed, as, whether he is a public officer, or a private member not in office, or whether the words are meant to be applied to his public conduct, or to his private character; and sometimes upon the degree of provocation, which the member speaking had received from the person he alludes to; and all these considerations must be attended to at the moment, as they are infinitely various and cannot possibly be foreseen in such a manner, that precise rules can be adopted with respect to them. 
When the Speaker observes upon any expression as personal and disorderly, and tending to introduce heat and confusion, and this appears to be the general sense of the house, the member offending ought immediately to make an apology, and to ask pardon of the house for his breach of their order, in as large and liberal expressions as possible, so as in such apology, to comprehend the person of whom the words were used. This is often very difficult to be obtained, especially when the offending person thinks he had sufficient provocation for using the expressions objected to. This consideration ought to be a warning to the house, and particularly to the Chair, to interfere at first; and not to permit any expressions to pass from a member unnoticed, which being applied by any other member as personally offensive to himself, may draw forth further words of heat and contumely, till at last confusion arises-different members take a warm and eager part in the dispute-and, besides the time that is lost in composing these differences, the House of Commons exhibits a scene of indecency and disorder, not very becoming their character as gentlemen, much less as one of the component parts of the great council of the nation assembled in parliament.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, February 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 9, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act.

Mr. Speaker, last night I was in the process of speaking to the second reading of the amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. I was not able to conclude my speech, on account of the time reaching ten o'clock. When I adjourned the debate I was talking about the necessity of paying some attention to the establishment of the family farm. I do not know that I need pursue that subject to any great extent, but I was mentioning the fact that the two-price system which we propose would help to some small degree in assisting the small farms. It is quite obvious, Mr. Speaker, that this is entering into the realm of fiscal policy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when we talk of the wheat producers' problem we are always told by the Liberal supporters of the government that we have sold more wheat than usual, and they begin to boast of the markets they have been able to secure for the farmers' wheat. They also boast that the total farm
Canadian Wheat Board Act income is, perhaps, a little higher than in the past. It is all very well to talk in that strain, but it is also advisable to point out that while there is an element of truth in these contentions there is another element which must be considered, namely the question of what has been termed the "price squeeze", as a result of which the amount of income the farmer receives today does not go as far as it did some years ago. In consequence, even though there may be more or less satisfactory markets and the over-all income may be slightly higher, the farmers, because of the price squeeze, find themselves in a very precarious position; they find it very difficult to keep their heads above water and to survive without going into bankruptcy.
The boast of markets and the boast of overall income does not satisfy the farmer who is on the verge of bankruptcy. Let me remind hon. members of this, Mr. Speaker: Mr. J. H. Wesson, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, issued a statement in which he outlined some of the developments affecting agriculture in 1956, and speaking of this price squeeze he said, and I quote from his speech:
But even on the basis of these good sales many farmers did not break even on the year's operations. The continued high cost of things needed to operate a farm and to maintain the farm family was putting the farmer in an impossible position. The price he received for his grain and other agricultural products was too low to keep the average farmer out of debt.
This situation can be illustrated by reference to the farm income and cost figures for 1955. Cash farm income for Saskatchewan that year was only eight per cent above the level of 1946, but prices of things farmers buy were 52 per cent higher than in 1946. The improvement in income in 1956 will not bridge the gap between costs and prices as shown in 1955 figures. The result is that many farmers are dipping into reserves to keep going while other farmers are accumulating debts which will be extremely difficult to pay at present prices.
Mr. Speaker, when you think of that, and then think in terms of the small farmer, you will realize that the small farmer is in a position where he is just about bankrupt. The other day I got a letter from a farmer in my constituency. He is a small farmer, and he writes this way-I will quote from his letter:
What I really wanted to write to you about is this: What is to become of the small farmer in southern Alberta? Is it the policy of the government in Ottawa that these small land holders should give up, sell out and try to make a new home somewhere else? What chance would a man almost 50 years of age, who was born here and lived here all his life, have of finding work elsewhere?
I suppose he could dig ditches or gardens, but I doubt if he could make a living at it. Is it right that a man should have to give up his home just because he did not venture out and grab up a lot of land? Everything seems to be in favour of the big land owners. Banks will lend them money; machine companies will give them discounts, wheat quotas on big acreages give them more return, etc.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
I am not saying, Mr. Speaker, that a man should not acquire a large farm if he wishes to do so and if he is a successful farmer, but I am saying that the fiscal policies of the government in respect of the wheat grower should be such that the small farmer can keep out of debt, support a good farm family and receive an adequate income in return for what he produces.
There is one further thing I wish to say, Mr. Speaker, in respect to the wheat board, and that is with regard to the quota system.
I know it is difficult when we have such huge surpluses to move the grain as many would like it to be moved, but there does seem to me to be some discrimination in the matter of quotas at the various points throughout western Canada. I do believe that there should be some policy adopted whereby there would be, by the end of the crop year, an equalization of the quotas throughout the country. In making reference to this I do not wish it to appear that I want any quotas in some sections of the country pulled down to the level of a lower quota that may exist in other parts of the country. But it must be kept in mind that there does appear to be some discrimination at times.
For instance, I find that farmers at some points, where they have had as much as an 8-bushel quota, are not always dependent upon wheat for their income. We may have certain points where the farmers can go into other lines of production such as cattle or hogs and are not dependent upon wheat for their income. Yet it will be found that at those particular points the quotas have been as high as 7 or 8 bushels whereas at other points dependent upon wheat growing the quotas have been lower. These other points are wheat growing areas where the soil is suitable for the growing of wheat and the water condition is perhaps not suitable for the raising of cattle. Therefore the farmers at such points grow wheat exclusively and are dependent upon the income they receive from their wheat. Yet at some of these points the quotas have been as low as 5 bushels.
That does seem to be discrimination, especially when these particular points may not be very far away from each other, perhaps 30, 40 or 50 miles or in an adjacent community. That situation does not tend towards satisfaction among our farmers. Therefore I urge that some attention be given to the equalization of quotas by the end of the crop year, particularly at the present time when we have huge surpluses which may continue for a number of years.
I wonder whether I might put on the record a table given to me in answer to a question I asked some little while ago. The table


shows the number of delivery points throughout the western provinces and the quotas delivered. I could read it but I will not take the time if I may have it put on Hansard. It is a short document.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, before the question is put I should like to say a few words prompted by two statements made in the house on the first day of February. The first statement was made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and, as found at page 890 of Hansard, it reads as follows:
That is the main reason why, on every and all occasions, the board, strongly supported by the government, has resisted efforts to put the board into the money-lending business by making advances to producers against grain stored on farms. That is not the business of the wheat board and should not be its business. To put the wheat board

into the business of making farm advances is the surest way I know of playing into the hands of those who would like to wreck the board as an effective marketing agency . . .
I think that statement needs some consideration. First, may I say in no uncertain manner that we in the C.C.F. are wholly in support of the wheat board method of selling wheat. We believe that had the board not been operating for the past ten years prices would have tobogganed to a ridiculous level. We know that the farmers know that and will resist almost with ferocity any attempt from any source to do away with that system and will not allow themselves ever again to be forced to sell through the grain exchange.
To those of us who have produced grain for the past 45 years that would be unthinkable. We will never forget the years when we were obliged to sell our wheat in the fall. When the first few loads of wheat came in the prices started to fall and they fell steadily until all of the wheat was in the hands of the speculators. Then prices started upwards. The grain exchange was the greatest gambling institution in the world at that time.
However, having said that, should we set up the wheat board on a pedestal and say that its members are supermen who will always be right and must never be criticized, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce implied in his speech on February 1? Surely in a democratic country governments themselves should be subject to criticism even by their own supporters. That is all to the good and makes for better government.
One statement of the minister with which I must take issue is his statement that the board is strongly supported by the government. I am amazed at that statement. Does the minister suggest that the government has relegated all its authority to the board regarding every phase of the handling of wheat? I have always thought that when a board was set up by a government the government provided a policy and instructed the board as to that policy.
The minister states quite correctly that the board was set up to sell wheat. But does he mean to tell the house that the wheat board dictates policy to him. I think hon. members know the minister too well to believe that. The minister has shown too many times in the house just who the big boss is on the government benches.
The minister complains that farmers are asking the government to make cash advances on farm-stored grain and says that if the wheat board had to do this it would wreck the board. He makes this as a bald
Canadian Wheat Board Act statement without producing any facts to back up the statement, nor does he offer any alternative. Apparently he and the government have decided that the farmer needs no more consideration.
Two years ago the government allowed elevator companies to make use of offsite storage. This was a big help, especially in those districts which built skating rinks. Those districts fortunate enough to have skating rinks, or which built skating rinks on the strength of the idea that they would derive revenue from the storage of wheat, were helped a great deal in that the farmers in these favoured areas were able to deliver a much greater quota of wheat. For some reason or other the government has cancelled this arrangement without in any way providing additional inland storage.
The minister seems to be quite satisfied that the farmers are not doing too badly, and when they bring their problems to the government and ask that certain action be taken to remedy some of the conditions under which they find themselves the minister as much as says that they are trying to sabotage the wheat board.
What are the things that the farmers are asking the government to do? First, they have asked that cash advances be made for grain which is stored on the farm. Anybody who knows anything about wheat farmers in particular at this time knows that the cash shortage on the farms for the past number of years has been very acute. While the cost of production has been going up rapidly, many farmers have not received sufficient cash on the amount of wheat they were able to sell to carry on their day to day operations.
The second complaint is that they want a better quota system. They want a more equitable quota system. We find that at some shipping points last year, as has been mentioned by many other members during the course of the debate, the quota got up to 8 bushels while other points did not get above a 4 or 5 bushel quota. To give one instance, the village of Marsden in Saskatchewan had an 8 bushel quota last year. When I left home a little over a month ago they were already up to a four-bushel quota this year. But the very next village eight miles away got up to only five bushels last year and at the time I left they were only on a one-bushel quota for this year. When complaints were made last year with regard to the quotas the minister gave to the house a definite commitment, as I thought at the time, that the situation would be remedied when the next crop year came around. So far that has not been done.
In the third place the farmers ask that a transport controller should be appointed to

Canadian Wheat Board Act see that the movement of wheat is carried out as expeditiously as possible and that no shipping points will be discriminated against. So long as the minister takes the attitude that he is not going to appoint a transport controller and that he cannot find one, he himself is the one who is putting an extra load on the wheat board, though he complains that the board should not be loaded down by some of these requests that our farmers have been making.
Another matter of interest is that farmers who belong to the wheat pool point out that, owing to the way box cars are allocated between elevators, they often have to use elevators they do not want to use when they have gone to the trouble and expense of building their own elevator system. This year the Saskatchewan wheat pool is paying a cash patronage dividend of one cent per bushel on 1955-56 deliveries amounting to over $1J million : there is also credit to members' accounts at the rate of 13/16 cents a bushel, amounting to about $1J million. This sum is to be used for the revolving fund deduction. While this amount is not large it would be completely lost if that grain were delivered to the line elevator companies. The farmers are demanding that something be done by the transport controller in order to see that they can deliver to elevators of their own choice.
Farmers are asking for more internal storage space so that the movement of wheat can be speeded up and so that, instead of cars having to go all the way to the lakehead, they can be emptied several times in the same length of time it would take to haul them to the lakehead. They have pointed out that with the exception of Churchill there has been no building of inland elevators for many years.
I think it would be a wise precaution if the government built up a good-sized wheat bank, some of which could be held in interior elevators to ensure our customers of a plentiful supply of bread food at all times. The western plains have always been subject to cycles of wet and dry years. While we have been in a wet cycle now for a number of years, a dry cycle will most certainly come again, and if we do not have the wheat to sell -and we have been in that situation in the past-when our customers want it, we are going to lose some of those customers; and once we have lost a customer, it is not always easy to get him back again.
Farmers are also suggesting a two-price system, with a domestic price which would bear a relation to the prices of the things the farmer has to buy. The minister has stated that he was not in favour of the consumer subsidizing the grain producer. But

let me remind the minister and the government that during both world wars the wheat growers subsidized not only the people of Canada but our overseas allies as well.
When world war II was over the Agricultural Prices Support Act was passed and $100 million was voted to support farm prices. The farmers were told at that time that this was compensation for the low prices paid during the war years. Surely the government could go as far as to accede to the demand of the farm organizations that a domestic price for wheat be set at $2.25 per bushel. This action would not raise the price of bread more than one half a cent a loaf.
Almost every major wheat-producing country in the world has taken steps to keep the farmers in business except Canada. Here the farmer seems to be the forgotten man. There is a sharp contrast between what the United States is doing to keep her farmers solvent and on the farm and what is being done in Canada. Last summer I drove across North Dakota. On the outskirts of every town and village were rows and rows of granaries full of wheat owned by United States government agencies. When a United States farmer harvests his crop he can do one of two things. He can sell it to the government agency and get cash in full, or he can store it in his own bin and collect storage payment until he is ready to sell. If he is short of storage space the government will lend him money with which to build granaries. If it so happens that the government agency has no space available and the farmer wants to sell, the agency will measure his bins, pay him for the grain, seal the bin and put on it a sign showing that the grain in that bin now belongs to the government agency. This seems to me to be a very simple transaction, and as yet I have seen nothing in United States papers finding any fault with that operation.
This scheme provides the farmer with the cash with which to pay his bills, provide for his family and home, and carry on necessary improvements. The banks, oil dealers, grocers, implement dealers, et cetera get back the credits that they have extended and the economy runs smoothly. For the life of me I cannot understand why the federal government here in Ottawa continues stubbornly to refuse the request of farmers and their organizations to make living on the farm a little bit more secure.
We in the C.C.F., because we have put forward some of the demands of western farm organizations, have been called calamity howlers and cry-babies. John Wesson, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, can

by no stretch of the imagination be considered to be a calamity howler or a cry-baby. In speaking to the annual convention of the wheat pool on November 15 last year he said this:

Two things were necessary, he said. One was the acceptance by the government of the principle that farmers were entitled to a reasonable price for their farm products. But I also say that the lot of the farmer is not made easier in Saskatchewan by the socialist members who since 1945 have acted in this house as professional cry-babies.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

I wanted to commend him and his colleagues for the good job they have done and commend the minister for maintaining such men in their responsible positions.
I do not intend repeating those things that have already been capably expressed by other speakers in this group but there are two or three matters which I feel should be emphasized further.
I want to draw to the minister's attention the fact that some sections of Canada have not had justice with regard to quotas. Many hon. members have spoken about this matter. My territory in the Peace river country is one area that has not received justice in relation to quotas. Perhaps it is because of its isolated position. The Peace river country is a vast grain-producing empire some 250 miles northwest of the city of Edmonton. Frequently we have been left until the very last with respect to getting our wheat out. The wheat board has consistently followed the practice of filling orders especially for export from points that are nearer to the places of shipment overseas and as a consequence of this policy our territory in the Peace river has been left out. I imagine the same thing could be said of certain other areas but I feel there are ways of correcting this situation. In spite of the minister's declaration last year that those farmers who were on a small quota at that time would be brought up this year to something approaching the level of those enjoying the best quotas the farmers in my country are not receiving that treatment. I am not blaming the minister but this does point up the necessity of having an appointment made to the vacant position of transport controller
in order that something may be done to correct the situation that has been referred to so frequently during the course of this debate.
In most of the points in the north Peace river area the farmers are on a 2-bushel quota and even with such a low quota they cannot deliver because box cars have not been made available and many points have been plugged from the early part of the season. One reason not many orders have been placed in that area by the wheat board this year is that frost hit the country and there is a great deal of low-grade wheat, No. 5 and below. Perhaps the demand for that type of wheat has not been very great for export purposes or for feeding purposes in Canada. This, too, serves to point up the necessity of improving our storage situation. It seems to me that an area 250 miles away from the nearest inland storage elevator ought to be considered as a location for an elevator with a capacity of one and a half or two million bushels. This proposal is given considerable weight by the fact that shortly the Pacific and Great Eastern Railway will be linked up with the Northern Alberta Railway at Dawson Creek and much of the farmers' produce will be marketed on the west coast. That being the case, the use of the Edmonton internal storage elevator would be practically denied to our people in the Peace river country. It seems to me that the building of an elevator in that area which is so far isolated from the main centres would be nothing more than justice to the farmers who have pioneered that country and are making of it a great food producing empire for which the people of Canada should be thankful.
Another point in this connection is that the minister should reconsider his position with respect to off-site storage. There are many points up in that country that could use off-site storage and would provide it if they could obtain a licence. The granting of further licences ought to be considered by the minister. I would hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would give more favourable consideration than he has in the past to this request for an inland storage elevator located somewhere in the Peace river country. I am sure he would find upon careful study that the construction of an elevator there would not only be justified but would to a large extent relieve the situation under which the farmers in that area have to operate. As I said, they are isolated and therefore frequently are not given shipping orders from the wheat board to take care of the demands from overseas. The farmers in that area are finding it extremely difficult to pay their bills and

Canadian Wheat Board Act to keep their families supplied with food, clothing, fuel and the necessities of life. As a matter of fact they are finding it difficult to keep ahead of the sheriff in connection with machine purchases because they cannot market enough of their crops to provide them with money to meet their bills. The people in that territory would have a much better chance of earning a decent livelihood if more inland storage was provided through terminal elevators and off-site storage.
The forward-looking enterprise of the government of British Columbia in extending the Pacific and Great Eastern Railway, to connect with the Northern Alberta Railway at Dawson Creek is to be commended and this will be of great assistance to the farmers in the Peace river territory when the route is completed. I wish to pay tribute to that enterprise and the vision behind it.
I would like to say a word or two concerning the question of parity prices. Other speakers from the Social Credit group have presented arguments in favour of parity prices and there are only one or two points I want to emphasize. Other hon. members of this group have declared that the Social Credit party in this house favours the establishment of parity prices for farmers. I do not think anybody could sensibly argue that farmers are not entitled to parity prices. Certainly no one on the government side of the house could reasonably argue that farmers are less entitled to parity prices than are industrialists. Industrialists get parity prices; they set their prices and many of them are protected by government policy on tariffs and customs. I think it is unreasonable to argue that farmers are less entitled to parity prices than labour is entitled to the stabilization of wages and salaries. Hon. members on the government side of the house have favoured, as we have in this group, the stabilization of wages and salaries for labour, through measures such as unemployment insurance and that sort of thing. We have also given support and consent to measures granting the labouring people in this country the right to strike, to have collective bargaining and things of that nature which enhance their chances of receiving a fair return for their labour. Having protected all other segments of Canadian society, why in the name of common sense are we so loath to come to the aid of our farming population which produces the food we need to keep alive? The Minister of Trade and Commerce and others have argued that to grant parity prices to the farmers would mean we would have to subsidize those prices. As was said so well by the hon. member for Lethbridge last night, even if we have to subsidize farm


prices in order to achieve parity prices we would be perfectly justified in doing so. I strongly suspect that because farmers constitute only 15 or 16 per cent of the total population of Canada this is one reason their voice is not heard as well as it was heard when farmers constituted 80 per cent of the total population of this country.
There was a time in Canada's history when 80 per cent of the population was engaged in farming and in those days the farmer had a far better deal than he is getting today. Today with only 15 or 16 per cent of our population engaged in farming the farmer is lucky if he receives 7 per cent of the national income. That is not right, nor is it fair.
For a number of years the Social Credit group have been proposing in this house the adoption of a two-price system of marketing of Canadian farm products. That cry has now been taken up by farm organizations and even our friends of the C.C.F. now advocate it. We are glad of that because we do not feel we have any corner on the idea, not for one minute. We are happy to see them putting it forward rather than to take issue with them. We rejoice in that action because it is the only way we can ever get anywhere, that is to have a universal acceptance of the idea. We have suggested that the establishment of a two-price system would be a step toward the establishment of parity prices in this country.
There are two phases to the two-price system, as has already been suggested. One phase has to do with external marketing and I do not intend dealing with that this afternoon because it has been dealt with already by other speakers. The other phase has to do with internal marketing. It is well known that approximately 94 per cent of all farm production in Canada, exclusive of wheat, is consumed in Canada. However, the peculiar thing is that the 6 per cent that is exported governs the price of the 94 per cent consumed internally. That should never be; that is a completely wrong principle which denies fairness and justice and denies the principle of supply and demand.
Over and above that the Canadian people consume approximately 160 million bushels of our wheat, either in the form of bread and cereals or seed, but not feed for cattle. That 160 million bushels could be made a very important factor in the establishment of parity prices. Our suggestion is that since the wheat board has the control of the total supply of wheat it would be a simple matter to grant to that board the right to set parity prices on that portion of our grain which is marketed and consumed internally. If they had that right it would go a long way toward

the establishment of parity prices. There is no reason why that could not be done as it would not interfere in any way with the good work being done by the Canadian wheat board.
I know the minister and several others have expressed their opposition to the idea because they do not want the Canadian consumer to subsidize farm prices. Bless my soul, what are the consumers of Canada doing in connection with automobiles and electrical goods. They are paying a price set by a protected industry and this government is providing that protection through its policies. If that is good for the electrical industry, if that is good for the automobile industry, it ought also to be good for the farmer. My contention is that we would be justified in giving the wheat board the right to establish parity prices on all grains marketed inside Canada. If that were done No. 1 wheat would sell at approximately $2.37 per bushel which is the price which has been established as being the likely parity price, a price which would bear a fair relationship to the prices the farmer has to pay for what he buys.
If that were done what would be the result? Would it in truth be necessary for the consumers of Canada to subsidize the price? I do not look upon an increase in price due to costs as being a subsidy. Subsidies are taken out of taxation and paid over as compensatory payments to certain classes or groups, but this matter of charging a price which is fair and just is not subsidization in any sense.
It has been pointed out already, and I want to emphasize it, that if our farmers were granted a parity price for their wheat, for that portion which is used internally, it would not necessarily increase the price of bread by more than one-half cent per loaf. The reason for that is plain. Anyone who has taken the trouble to examine into the way costs have risen since 1945, labour costs, paper costs, packaging costs, retail marketing costs and so on, will have found that the great bulk of the increase in the prices of 16-ounce or 24-ounce loaves has been made up of the increases in things other than the cost of wheat. The fact is that the wheat content in a loaf of bread would not raise the retail price of a 16-ounce or 24-ounce loaf by more than one-half cent if parity prices were adopted.
Ask any person in this country who has the interests of the farmer at heart; ask the labouring man who works in industry what he would think of having to pay a half cent increase in the price of a loaf of bread, and I will guarantee that he would think it through and say: "I favour it because when
Canadian Wheat Board Act the farmer gets an increase in his wheat return he is going to buy more of the products of industry and that is going to stabilize my wages or salary position."
It is well known that in those years when the total volume of wages and salaries in industry has been approximately the equal of the total volume of farm cash income there has been no unemployment, the country has been considered to be prosperous and everybody has been happy. But just let farm cash income begin to decline below the volume of industrial salaries and wages and it will not be long until those industrial salaries and wages will follow the decline and someone will be out of a job. Labour favours the establishment of parity prices for farmers because they know that the farmers constitute their best markets for industrial goods and that their chances of remaining in good jobs with decent wages depend to a large degree upon whether the farmer can buy what is being produced.
Under those circumstances and with those facts in mind I submit that we are not justified in doing anything else but give the wheat board the right to set the internal price at parity for all farm products consumed internally. So far as the external part of the parity price system is concerned, I agree that it would be necessary to establish a floor below which we would not allow that price return to go. However, that is another matter. Even so I think we would be perfectly justified in establishing parity prices all the way through in order to stabilize our economy and insulate us against the sharp declines that are bound to take place when farm cash income does not come up to the required level.
I think that is about all I wish to say at the moment in that connection, but there are two things I should like to deal with very briefly in rebuttal. Mr. Speaker, I was in the process of explaining why we support the Canadian wheat board and the present bill when I was interrupted at one o'clock. I would just like to take one or two minutes in which to finish what I had to say and then to help the minister get his bill through if we can.
In the first place, the Canadian wheat board was established as a consequence of the demands of the overwhelming majority of the wheat producers in western Canada for a marketing board of that type. It was not imposed by the government upon the farmers. It was given to them as a result of a request for such a board. That is the first important thing. It seems to me that when the overwhelming majority of the producers in any division request some form of marketing service which will be theirs, we have no alternative but to grant it to them if we can.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
Mr. Speaker, the wheat board has continued to operate as an agency representing the producers themselves and certainly in no way can be considered to be a government agency imposed upon the farmers. That is quite distinct from the kind of thing that the socialists would do. The socialists would not wait for the producers in any division to express their desire to have a marketing board of this kind. If they took it into their heads to do so, they would impose it by compulsion on those producers, just as they did in the case of the lumber board in Saskatchewan. The difference between the two ideas, the two types of marketing agency, is this. In the case of the wheat board, having been requested by the producers and having been granted control over 100 per cent of that type of production, the board goes ahead and markets and pays back to the producers the total of the moneys taken in the process of marketing the goods, less perhaps some of the costs of the service of marketing. In the second place it was imposed by the government as a compulsory service, whether the people wanted it or not. In the third place-
You can sell your own lumber.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my purpose to say more than a few words in closing this debate. As I have said before, the bill is very simple. The effect of its provisions is to make three changes in dates in the bill, from August 1, 1957 to August 1, 1962. That is the whole purpose of the bill.
I opened by making a few remarks about the wheat board. We have heard the spokesmen for all three parties say that they favour the bill. I think there is every evidence that the Liberal party is unanimously in favour of the bill and I am satisfied that the official opposition is in favour of the bill. The suggestion has been made that the board should make payments on farm-stored grain.
In that the official opposition differs from the other parties because, I noted, the other parties say someone other than the wheat board should make advances on farm-stored grain. I would like, Mr. Speaker, to correct the impression which the socialists are trying to convey that the board is a great socialist experiment operated by the government. That is totally untrue. The wheat board method of marketing antedates the socialist party. I do not think there was a socialist in Canada when the wheat board method of marketing was originated in 1924 or 1925. Until the depression came along to interfere with its functioning, the board operated entirely as a voluntary organization of prairie farmers running their own business of selling wheat. The only difference between the board as it functioned then and as it functions now is that the government nowadays guarantees the finances used by the board in carrying on its operations. And, more recently, it has taken over part of the wheat pool surplus and is carrying it on government account. That is the only difference, and to claim that the board is socialistic, or that it has any particular love of or tie with socialists is completely false.
The board is a farmers' board. Operating expenses of the board are paid by the farmers themselves. The board is advised by an advisory board made up entirely of producers and producer organizations. Moreover, the authority for setting the price of grain is vested in the board and not in the government-it has been vested by this parliament in the board itself. Let us, therefore, get rid of the idea that there is anything socialistic about the wheat board.

Mr. Speaker, 1 said I believed that the official opposition favour this bill. I do not believe for a moment that the socialists favour the bill. They say they favour the bill, but- just sit down-what did they say about the wheat board?

I would like to know on whose authority, or on what statement made in the house, the minister can base the ridiculous statement that members of the C.C.F. party do not favour the principle of the orderly marketing of wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I will be glad to elucidate. The marketing of Canadian grain is essential to the Canadian economy. I am sure that is true. And we think that a market for Canadian grain must be preserved-a market which will return the value of Canadian grain to the Canadian economy. The United States is in a different position. The United States was never an important factor in the world market for wheat until towards the end of the second world war. The economy of the United States does not depend on the export of wheat. Through internal policies the United States has built up production of wheat in excess of its requirements, and it has undertaken to market that surplus wheat in a way which we believe is destructive of Canadian markets and of the position of Canadian wheat on the world market.
We have protested about these methods. The socialists tell us these methods of United States selling are right. Several speakers, both in the Social Credit party and in the C.C.F. party, say that is the way to market wheat. Do they mean to tell me that a man who is supporting the wheat board in Canada would make that statement? Could anything be more ridiculous? We have heard a good many strange statements, particularly from the C.C.F. party, and I hope the people in the prairies will read these speeches which C.C.F. members have been making. If they do I think we will have fewer C.C.F. members in the next house than we have in the present house.
A lot less.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not know that the disagreement with the United States about marketing methods has any particular place in this discussion. As I say, I have protested about others talking about everything but the bill and the wheat board, and I think, perhaps, I had better keep to the text.
There is one matter I might deal with, and that is the question raised by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) as to why Alberta grain cannot be bought 82715-711
Canadian Wheat Board Act directly from farmers by feeders in British Columbia. This act provides that the wheat board shall be the sole marketing agency for wheat in the designated area, that is, in the prairie provinces. You may say that it is not the sole marketing agency because one farmer can sell to another-in other words, that a farmer can be a marketing agency. Well, we try to carry out the intention of the act that the wheat board should be the sole marketing agency, and in doing so we use every method consistent with the powers of the federal government.
We can legally prevent wheat moving across interprovincial borders; we can prevent wheat moving across the international border; we can prevent wheat not marketed through the wheat board moving on the railways; and we can prevent wheat not under the control of the wheat board being received at government elevators and feed mills which are agents of the wheat pool. We do all that. But we cannot prevent one farmer selling to another farmer within the same province. Only the government of the province itself can do that. Each province has, in the case of barley and oats, passed legislation regulating sales within the province. However, this government cannot do it, and we do not attempt to stop it-in other words, as far as we are concerned it is legal for one farmer to sell to another farmer within a province.
Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I would prefer he did not interrupt me in the middle-
I understand you to say that the provinces had all passed legislation to prevent one farmer selling oats and barley to another. That is strictly not the case, is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
However, the
point I am making is that so far as it lies within federal authority we carry out the spirit of the act. For that reason it is not possible for any individual to take wheat across a provincial border. No individual can do that legally under the provisions of the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
A farmer can buy wheat from the wheat board. He does not get the discount that a farmer in distress may be willing to give on wheat for which he needs quick cash. I think farmers are realizing more and more that it

Canadian Wheat Board Act is not good business to discount their wheat too quickly for the sake of a quick sale.
That is the situation, and I would like to make it clear. There are certain farmers in British Columbia, within the designated area, who have protested that they cannot take their wheat to Vancouver. They could-if they could do it without crossing an interprovincial border. But we do not ask those farmers to stay in the designated area. We are quite willing to remove those districts in British Columbia from the designated area and let them sell their wheat where they like. We have put that proposal to them, and it has been turned down unanimously as far as I can find out. But in dealing with the wheat board they must take the good with the bad and obey the rules, and that applies to the farmers of British Columbia just as it applies to the farmers of the prairie provinces.
The wheat board has a very difficult job. It is attempting to maintain order in world markets for wheat. It is attempting to maintain a stable price in world markets, and it is being undercut in many of those markets by competitors who do not have the same desire for stability. Happily we have maintained the price and at the same time have been able to sell something like our proportion of world markets. We think that when the United States wheat surplus is disposed of and the Americans retire from the markets, as they are pretty sure to do unless the subsidy on American wheat is continued indefinitely, we will have a world market on which Canada can trade as she did in earlier days. But it is a very difficult job and every discussion we have here in the house always has a depressing effect on the sale of wheat. For example, the suggestion is made that we should follow the American practice and put wheat afloat unsold that can be offered through brokers at prices lower than the market price. Every suggestion of that kind makes the task of the wheat board more difficult and is always reflected in the sales of wheat for a period after these debates take place.
In my opinion we have gone far afield in this debate. We have taken up matters that have no reference whatever to the proposal I am making to the house, and I think the wheat board has been the sufferer as a result. I do not know what we can do about wheat legislation. Last year I had a reasonably simple bill requested by a great number of people from the prairies. It was filibustered here for weeks. This is the fourth day of debate on this very simple bill to change a date. I have another bill in mind that should be put through at this session and I think that legislation I have in mind will be required. A great many people on the prairies

But I think the idea that we can tie up the House of Commons for weeks to change a date in an act just because the bill refers to wheat is a theory that is untenable.

I want to take this opportunity to bring two questions to the attention of the minister upon which I have been asked to get information. As I have mentioned before, the dairymen, poultrymen and livestock feeders in my constituency find that the cost of feed is a very high proportion of their costs, in fact it is twice the normal Canadian average. The cost of feed to these producers in my constituency is about 40 per cent of their selling price, whereas the normal Canadian average is about 20 per cent, so I am sure the minister will appreciate what a serious thing this cost of feed is to my constituents.
This matter was discussed quite completely at the last annual convention of the B.C. federation of agriculture. Two things were discussed, the high cost of feed and the possibility of buying direct from the farmer through the wheat board in order to save the handling costs. Then, there was another question, and that was the refusal of the railways to load grain within the province for transportation to another point in the province, as a result of instructions from the wheat board. In that connection, I want to read very briefly from Country Life, which deals with a report of that convention:
Questions Authority
There is a feeling among some agricultural producers in this province that the Canadian wheat board is operating beyond its legal powers when it controls rail shipments of feed grains within the province, as in the case of the Creston movements.
I might say in that connection that producers in my constituency had repeatedly tried to purchase grain in that area but the railway company would not accept it for loading because of some rulings of the wheat board. I continue the quotation:
This was expressed by central Vancouver island poultry producers' association when it received unanimous endorsation of a resolution calling for the B.C. attorney-general to study wheat board practices and to proceed to obtain judgment from the courts if he finds that the wheat board is acting without legal authority.
My two questions to the minister are as follows: Is it possible, owing to the circumstances of many producers in British Columbia with respect to the high cost of feed, for some arrangement to be made for purchases direct from the farmers through the wheat board, that is to save handling costs between

Canadian Wheat Board Act the farmer, the elevator and so on? Then again, what authority has the wheat board to prevent the railroads loading grain within a province for transportation to another point within the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The answer to the first question is that it is not possible to buy direct from the farmer through the wheat board. It is possible to buy direct from the wheat board at any marketing point in the province, that means any country elevator, and the purchase price there is the export price at Vancouver less the freight costs charged for the movement from that point to Vancouver. This purchase is legal and afterwards the grain bought in that way will have a certificate that lets it be moved anywhere and by any vehicle.
The reason the railroads cannot accept a shipment of wheat is the provision in the act that we are now extending. That provision has recently been tested in the courts. The case was taken to the Supreme Court of Canada and the court upheld the regulation of the wheat board, so I think that has been settled by the highest court in the land that it is not legally possible.

Further to what I said earlier in this debate and following what the hon. member who just took his seat had to say, I have a question I should like to pose to the minister. During the course of the debate I proposed he set up a fact-finding board to discover if there is any means whereby we can, without circumventing the wheat board, because we in British Columbia realize the value of boards, stop this discrimination between the various provinces, or within the province itself, as a result of the sale of wheat at fire-sale prices.
No one wishes to have grain or any other products sold on the basis of a fire-sale price. We are fully aware of the need for the wheat board, and for this reason we have such boards in my own province. However, I do question whether we will not find ourselves in an awkward position in the very near future if we should have all grain go through the wheat board, as it undoubtedly would, and a short crop year should come to this country. It would appear to be a blessing as far as the farmer is concerned. The wheat board would be able to get rid of the grain by reason of our having a short crop year, and this would give the farmer an opportunity to get ready cash. The farmers on the prairies could go into the poultry business; but we in British Columbia would be in the awkward position of not having these goods supplied to us.
(Mr. Herridge.]
I would like to know if the minister has examined the possibility of setting up a factfinding board to determine what would be the long-range effects of this act. The act has been in operation long enough to enable us to assess its immediate effects, and we certainly can observe them; but has he given any thought at all to the long-range effects?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: When this act was passed, Mr. Chairman, parliament made it clear that the wheat board was to be the sole marketing agency for Canadian wheat. I should not like to take any step that would weaken the position of the board in that respect. They enforce the intent of the act as far as they can.

One further matter, Mr. Chairman. I can fully appreciate the minister's point. It is not my intention to suggest that the wheat board's position should be weakened in any way. What I am proposing is that the act should be examined to see if it could be extended in order to make it stronger.
I believe the hon. member for Lethbridge, in speaking the other day, brought out a point that might be the answer to the whole problem. If there were cash advances for feed grain, seed grain or grain of any kind stored on the farms the problem would not arise, because the farmer would not have to sell his grain at fire-sale prices.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, possibly it would be helpful if the minister would explain the basis upon which the administration decided to extend the period for five years. At one time, as I recall it, the extension was for three years and on the second occasion it was for four years. What is the reason for extending the period of five years at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not know that there was any particular reason. The country seems to be getting used to the wheat board and it did not seem necessary to have this discussion come up as often as it did in the early stages. Our machinery of marketing is becoming adjusted to the wheat board system. There was no particular sanctity about the five years, and if anyone wanted to suggest some other period we would be glad to consider it. It seemed to the government that five years was a reasonable period.

Mr. Chairman, I support this amendment because I believe the Canadian Wheat Board Act should be a permanent act and not subject to repeal, revision or expiry at a given date. I have always supported the wheat board. I looked up the very first speech I made in this house on February 16, 1936, and before dealing with the matter then before the house, I had this say, as reported on page 175 of Hansard of that date:
Under the last administration-

-a wheat board was established, and that board was satisfactory to the producers of western Canada; the resolutions of the organized producers show that, I think, completely. Since hon. gentlemen opposite have taken office very disquieting events have occurred.

I do not want to leave the matter for revision or expiry in the hands of governments which may prove again to be unfriendly to the wheat board method of marketing. I was here during the whole of that controversy and I remember most definitely that the original basis of the wheat board was undermined by the present administration. When they have the nerve to stand up in this house and accuse those of us who through the years have supported the wheat board method of marketing of trying to undermine and destroy the wheat board, I say that that is slander and when it is written, libel on a group of people who have been wholeheartedly in favour of it.
To suggest that there are today any members of this house who oppose the wheat board at this time is equally slanderous, as the vote this afternoon will show. I resent very much the implications by people in this house who try to say that we are opposed to this method of marketing. In fact we want to see it extended to rye and flax and to have a system of orderly marketing set up for all farm products as the producers desire it. It should not be something inflicted upon them, but as they wished it. There should be such a system of orderly marketing under properly constituted boards for all farm products.
My memory is quite good about the long debates which took place between 1935 and 1940 when the war broke out. Then we got the marketing of wheat completely under the control of the wheat board, something we did not have before. I would like to see this act on the statute books as a permanent piece of legislation so that there may be no ifs and buts about it in the days to come.

Mr. Chairman, on this clause and on the amendment I think it is important that the government should make some statement of policy in regard to its position in connection with the transport controller. This particular clause relates to the loading of grain into railway cars. I think we have had an adequate discussion of this principle in the past. As pointed out by members of the government, the office of 

transport controller is a necessary one. In its annual report the Canadian wheat board referred to the problems confronting it in allocating box cars to marketing points. In view of the fact that it has received the support of members of this house over and over again when extensions have been asked for in the tenure of the board, having regard to the support which farmers in general have given to orderly marketing, I see no reason why this amendment should not be supported. It will be interesting to find out the degree to which my hon. friends who support the Liberal party will indicate their support of and belief in the wheat board when the vote takes place on the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, as the leader of this group said in the discussion on second reading, he was not opposed to the board being made permanent but he saw certain advantages in the bill under discussion in that when the expiry date was reached we would review the operations of the wheat board. Right here may I say that I do not think the Minister of Trade and Commerce need be too alarmed at the scope of the debate we had on second reading. It is true as he said that this is a simple bill which extends the life of the board for another five years, but we were debating the principle of the

bill. Therefore we had the right to say, "Do we want the wheat board to continue for five years, or do we not?" It did open up the whole matter of the wheat board, and rightly so, I think. 1 do not blame the minister for being concerned at the political trend of the debate, because he had some reason.
In respect to the amendment, I am willing to support it because I see no reason why the wheat board should not be made permanent. At the same time I do not think the amendment is as serious as some might indicate, because it is a matter of fact that in law nothing is permanent. As a matter of fact, though it may seem paradoxical to say it, the wheat board is permanent for the next five years. The leader of the C.C.F. party has said he wants it to be made permanent because he does not know what might happen should a government come into power which is not too favourable toward the board. Well, the result would simply be this. Even though the act were made permanent, any government which came into power which did not like it could repeal the measure. So it does not make any difference, and I cannot work up any enthusiasm one way or another as to whether it should be extended for five years or made permanent.
However, I have no objection to the amendment and I am quite willing, personally, to vote for permanency.

Mr. Chairman, I said earlier in this debate that I thought 99 per cent of the farmers in the west today support the wheat board, and I presume that is one of main reasons the minister has brought this measure forward on this occasion. But that does not mean that farmers five years from now will still feel the same way about it. Conditions can change, and I think it is sensible to have the matter reviewed in five years and hear what the attitude of the farmers is at that time.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said today that no one is opposed to the wheat board, as demonstrated by the vote in the house. That is true, but I still find it strange that a party which is so strongly in favour of the wheat board has been, for five days, criticizing just about everything the wheat board has done.

May I offer an explanation which I think will make the amendment clear to the hon. member and all other members of the committee. Reference has been made to clause 1 of the bill, which has been disposed of. That dealt with part II of the Canadian Wheat Board Act which is entitled "Control of elevators and railways." We are now dealing with a clause that relates to section 24 of the act, which is the first section in part III which is entitled "Interprovincial and export marketing of wheat by board."
In other words, what we are now aiming to do is to make permanent the part of the wheat board act that has to do with the marketing of wheat by the Canadian wheat board. I realize that my hon. friend has not a copy of the statute before him at the moment, but may I tell him that at the present time section 24 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act reads as follows:
24. Subject to section 31, in this part "pool period" means
(a)	each crop year subsequent to the 31st day of July. 1950, and prior to the first day of August, 1957; and
(b)	thereafter, such period or periods as parliament may fix for such purpose.
