speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That It is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources Act to provide for the establishment of two national museums in lieu of one, as at the present time to be known as the Canadian museum of natural history and the Canadian museum of human history.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have just a few words to say in explanation of the resolution. In the course of its development to the position of national importance it now holds, the national museum of Canada has assumed a function for which its present organization is now no longer entirely appropriate. To rectify this it is proposed to establish two museums. As the minister, under the present act, does not have the power to establish museums, the proposed amendment would give him that power.
In the organization of the national museum there is a definite division between the different parts of the work relating to human history, including the fields of archaeology, anthropology and ethnology, and those parts relating to natural history including geology, botany and zoology. In 1951 the royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences studied the work of the national museum, and concluded that its organization did not make adequate provision for the best possible development of each of these two main divisions. The commission proposed that to provide for full development in the future of the museum functions in the fields of both human and natural history two museums, one to deal with human history and one with natural history, should be created from the existing museum. By such a reorganization and subsequent expansion of activities the two national museums would be able to make their full contribution to Canadian life.
Until recently it would not have been practicable, because of space limitation, to make the change. We can now see, however, that within three years new building programs in the Ottawa area will make possible the move from the present Victoria memorial museum building of both the national gallery and the geological survey, thereby increasing by three times the space now available. With this great improvement in the space situation

Northern Affairs and National Resources
in sight and with the enormous amount of planning and exhibit preparation that must be done to make ready tor this, the time has now become opportune to carry out the anticipated reorganization as recommended by the Massey commission.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext: I was not quite clear as to what the minister meant, Mr. Chairman, when he started his remarks on this subject by saying that the present museum set-up is no longer appropriate. I hope we might get a little explanation of what he meant by those words.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext: The organization set-up-

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
He has stated as his only reason for introducing this bill to form two museums instead of one the fact that such a course was recommended by the Massey report. I do not think the fact that it was so recommended should be taken as a sufficiently good reason in itself for legislation of this sort. After all, a considerable number of things were recommended in that report which the government has not seen fit to implement. Recently another report, the Gordon report, has been received and if one can judge from the remarks made by some, particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce, it would seem evident that the government is not going to implement the recommendations in that report. Therefore the fact that a certain recommendation is made in a certain report cannot be taken, in itself, as sufficient reason for passing legislation.
The minister concluded by saying that within three years' time space will be available in the present building as a result of the removal from that building of certain branches of other departments which have been occupying it for some time. I know that so far as the museum is concerned, space has been very much at a premium. This has been one of the great difficulties. I am glad to hear that more space will be available and that the present building, which was built as a museum, will be available for use as a museum. However, since both these projected museums are going to be in the same building, I find it somewhat difficult to understand why we need legislation to set up two separate museums. I should like to know whether the curator of the museum has found it impossible to carry on his duties, and whether there is any necessity for dividing the functions between two curators, thereby doubling the expense. I would doubt very much whether that is the case.
As to the necessity of forming two museums which would be under the same roof, apparently the great museums which exist in the various countries of the world have
not found that necessary. The British museum is an example of the fact that it is not necessary to divide this into two or three museums. If these museums were to be in two separate buildings there would appear to me to be more justification for setting up two museums in place of one. Since all the museum facilities are apparently to be housed in the one building, and since nothing has been advanced by the minister so far to indicate that one curator and one museum would not be adequate, possibly divided into two or more branches-in fact I think perhaps the museum should be divided into three or four branches dealing with different types of material-I can see no real reason for the introduction of this legislation. After all, the two museums will continue to be really one museum in one building. It would seem to me a matter of duplication and an increase in what you might call administrative responsibilities. I would think the extra money involved would be much better devoted to securing more specimens for the museum.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
I welcome the announcement by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources because, as an individual, I find nothing more enjoyable than being able to spend an afternoon in a museum. I have been disappointed on visits to the museum in Ottawa to find it very crowded, and to find much of the space in that building occupied by the geologicial branch of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. These departments take up space which could very well be filled with displays concerning some phases of our past history which visitors to the museum would find very interesting.
I think the decision to divide it into two branches is desirable, because it will give the branch of the museum dealing with human history an opportunity to explore more extensively the past history of Canada and to display its findings. There have been several field expeditions in various parts of Canada exploring civilizations that have existed on this continent in past centuries. I believe this legislation will make it possible for more extensive expeditions to go into the field. Unless we explore the various sites of which we have knowledge while we still know where they are located it will not be too many decades before the sites have disappeared and those portions of the record of history will be lost forever.
Another important point arising from the introduction of this resolution is that we will have an opportunity to take out of storage many of the findings of former field expeditions, since there will be room in the

Northern Affairs and National Resources museum to display them. I hope that as a result of this resolution we will have here iri Ottawa as a national museum an institution which will favourably compare with the Royal Ontario museum in Toronto.
We have an excellent museum located in Regina, and have received favourable comments about it from people who have had an opportunity of visiting there. I welcome this endeavour by the minister to establish a museum of natural history and a museum of human history, so that as Canadians we may be proud of our display of history and as individuals we may have a knowledge of and an interest in what has occurred in the past.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is necessary for me to dwell on this subject at great length, but I should like to point out to the minister that I feel here is a great deal of merit in the resolution he is proposing today. As has already been indicated by previous speakers, it will be a good thing to establish a national museum on an extended basis.
I am wondering, though not in a critical way, what will be the added cost involved. I understand that both the museum of Canadian natural history and the museum of human history will be housed in the one building. The building will require a certain amount of renovation, and though I would not imagine that the cost will be great I think we should have some indication as to what it might be. Of course there will also be the additional cost of providing the separate staffs that will be neceessary, and we should have some indication of that cost.
It seems to me there is a great deal of work to be done in preserving both our natural history and our human history, and I would think some attention should be paid to giving assistance to museums in other parts of the country that maintain the record of our history. My mind goes at once to my own constituency. A museum has been established in the city of Drumheller under vast difficulties. I do not suppose there is an area in Canada which holds greater prospects for field expeditions exploring the record of the past than the so-called badlands of Drumheller, where the remains of nearly all the prehistoric animals have been found. Wonderful work has been done by the small museum in Drumheller, which has unearthed discoveries that are thousands and thousands of years old.
Many donations have been made to that museum. Although I have referred to it as a small museum I should qualify that by saying it is not small in relation to the size of Drumheller, but only when we think of museums in the national sense. I think it

would be wrong to concentrate all our efforts on the construction of a national museum at the expense of ignoring the efforts being made by museums in other places to preserve our history.
There is an excellent museum located in the town of Banff, which I am sure the minister has visited. I understand the work of this museum is carried on entirely through donations received from private individuals. I have gone through that museum on a number of occasions, and they have many wonderful displays of animal and natural life. Practically all the wild animals are on exhibit there. I am sure no one who visits the national park, and there are many thousands each year who do, fails to visit the museum. I venture to suggest that just as many people visit the Banff museum as visit the museum in Ottawa, if not more. Many thousands of people go through the museum during the tourist season, and you can hardly enter the building because of the crowds.
Although I am by no means belittling the proposal contained in this resolution, I think some attention should be given to assisting museums in other areas where the local people have taken a keen interest in preserving historical treasures. If the minister would give consideration to the museums at Banff and Drumheller I am sure it would enable them to make a further contribution to the preservation of historical records, and thus assist the national museum.
I want to assure him that I think he is following a wise course in introducing this resolution, and I trust he will see his way clear to extending his thinking to museums and activities beyond the scope of those mentioned in this legislation.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF TWO NATIONAL MUSEUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak briefly in approval of the principle of this resolution. It seems to me the principle is entirely in keeping with the growth and development of Canada during recent years.
I do not suppose there is anyone in this chamber who has not taken advantage of the opportunity to make a tour of the national museum during his years in Ottawa and certainly none of us would fail to agree that it was a most instructive and interesting experience. But I remember that on the first occasion-not the last occasion but the first- when I made a tour of the museum, I came to the end of the tour feeling, "Is this all?" It seemed to me that for a country of the present status of Canada there should have been something more; it should have been a more extensive establishment. For that reason I think the proposal to divide the

Private Bills
museum into two separate branches will enable a great deal of development to take place in each branch.

Mr. Speaker, I was quite interested when I read this bill to find one significant omission from the list of wholly-owned subsidiaries of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Mr. Speaker, I have been quite interested in this bill because it seems to me to be almost a classic example of the sort of thing against which I and my colleagues in this house have been protesting against for years. I was interested the other day to hear the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre remark that the socialists usually did not have much connection with business, and I would be the first to agree with him. Socialists, like other intelligent people, do have some doubts as to the wisdom of devoting the short period during which we are on this earth to the business of buying things cheaply and selling them dearly, whether it be selling hardware-in Moose Jaw or embarking on wider areas of rapacity and dealing in oil and natural resources of various kinds.
We are asked to believe, Mr. Speaker, that the promoters and owners of the present company wish to take this action in order to-distribute the shares of their holdings among the general public. Now I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when they ask us to believe that they insult our intelligence. In the first place, if this were so they would be almost the first promoters in history to decide that they wished to invite the public in, unless their enterprise was in a shaky condition or they hoped for some stock market scheme whereby they would gain big profits.
But in this instance the case is clear cut; this is just nonsense, and dishonest nonsense, that is being told to us in this regard; because if the people who had formed this company had wished to have the public participate, then it seems very odd that of the 5 million shares of no par value which were authorized!

in 1951 only some 1 million-odd have been issued, and of that 1 million only 450,000 were made available to the general public.
We are told that another reason why they want to split the stock is that the price has gone so high that the general public is unable, or unwilling, to engage in trading in that stock. Again I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that the price had gone so high only in the last year since it became obviously an extremely profitable undertaking. There were two years in which it was not nearly so high, but these gentlemen made no effort at that time to attempt to sell some of the shares, amounting to nearly 3J million, which they had in their company treasury. They waited until the exorbitant profits which were shown last year caused the price of their stock to rise to its present dizzy and encouraging height.
Then it was decided that they wanted to split the stock five to one in order to permit the general public to participate in their operations. But we have had no indication whatever from the sponsor of this bill that the company does actually intend to sell to the public any of those 3J million shares- they would become 16 million shares-which are in their treasury. We have no undertaking to that effect.
We have, indeed, the possibility that what will happen is that those who own the present shares will decide to cash in on their profits after the shares have been split and traded on the stock market until their price has reached an encouraging level. These gentlemen may then unload some of their holdings; they may, indeed, initiate a regular campaign of unloading with the idea of resuming possession of the stock later on.
I cannot imagine for the life of me, Mr. Speaker, how anyone could consider that there is a respectable reason for this proposition which is, of course, just the well-known old racket of melon-cutting. And this parliament is being asked to enable that to be done.
There are those, of course, who imagine that the capital gains that would accrue to these gentlemen would come out of thin air. My friends to the left will probably think that. But I would like to assure them and other hon. members of this house that this is not the case, and that the capital gains which will be made by these people will come out of thje pockets of their fellow Canadian citizens. Let no one try to tell you anything different. If this parliament permits this bill to go through, then they are permitting these gentlemen to draw their capital gains from the pockets of the Canadian public; and I would suggest to all those hon. members of

this house who have been making heartwarming speeches about the necessity for providing more for our old age pensioners, increased family allowances and larger sums in the way of general social security benefits, that they bear in mind that the economy of Canada can carry just so much of a load. It can carry just so much in the way of profits for stock market racketeers; and with every dollar of capital gain that we permit by this scandalous and iniquitous proposal we will lessen the area from which help for the less fortunate members of our society may come.

They have in the main done very well out of the people of Canada and their natural resources. I see no reason why parliament should aid them to do well out of the people of Canada by means of a stock market racket of this barefaced nature. Since the amendment moved by my colleague the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was ruled out of order, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam:
That Bill No. 15 be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

Mr. Speaker, in my opinion the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Nanaimo certainly should go a long way to fneeting the suggestions made when the bill was being debated earlier that an opportunity should be given to members to have placed before them all information that could be made available. In a matter of this kind I think the approach suggested in the amendment is a much more appropriate way to deal with the question than for us to be compelled to accept the principle of the bill and then go into committee to get the information that may be required.
The information placed on the record by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam at an earlier stage of the debate was brought into serious and, I thought, unnecessary question by one or two who took part in the debate. Suggestions were made that he had pulled some figures out of a hat and had used
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo).)
them loosely. I suggest that was a rather unwarranted approach to take to the matter, because we all know that reliable figures with respect to earnings and other matters concerning companies do appear from time to time and are available for the use of those who have occasion to discuss matters relating to the operations of firms or the nature of transactions that are being proposed. I think perhaps it was a little unfair to suggest that the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam had not taken the pains to go to sources that he considered reliable in order to obtain the information he used.
I have no real quarrel with the fact that other hon. members may place a different interpretation upon the facts or may have a different view of their implications than the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam; nevertheless I feel that it was not a proper approach to take in a serious discussion of this measure.
This company have come before parliament seeking approval for a certain action which they contemplate taking, and I certainly think we have a right and a responsibility to inquire seriously into all the implications of their request. I am aware of the fact that long before I came into the house a great many debates took place on a number of pipe-line questions and that, of course, the original incorporation of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company was a matter of discussion in the house. If the company is going to request the kind of change in their operations suggested in the bill now before us, I believe the house should have the right and the opportunity to go into the history of the operations of the company before we decide whether or not we approve the principle of what they are doing.
There are probably members in the house who are prepared to accept without question as a general principle the right of a company to split its shares as it pleases. I do not happen to subscribe to that view. 1 think the whole approach to the making of unearned wealth, which in my opinion has been followed all too commonly by many companies and corporations in this country, is basically wrong. As far as I am concerned the onus should be upon the company to prove beyond any shadow of a doubt that the proposal they have in mind is necessary and justified.
I think a good deal of confusion exists in the minds of a lot of people as to the basis on which proper earnings should be made by a corporation. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said, we in this group take the view that under certain circumstances companies which are operating

efficiently and without damage to the public interest have the right to a reasonable return on their investment.
We also take the view that in certain fields of operations where high risks are involved, those risks rightly should give entitlement to more generous treatment than would be legitimate in other fields. I feel that this applies particularly to the field of the basic development of mines and of oil producing wells. No one will quarrel with the fact that in their initial stages at least such ventures are more risky than are many other types of operations. But I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that a debate on the pros and cons of what is a proper return on invested capital or a proper return for risks which are taken is an altogether different matter from this business of making speculative profits through the manipulation of stocks on the market.
I may perhaps be subject to prejudice in this matter, but certainly my opinions in this regard are not of recent origin. In the days of 1928 and 1929, when in my view the world had gone a bit crazy or at least the people on this continent had done so in respect of gambling in stocks, I can recall the views I came to then, and they are substantially the views I continue to hold. I mention that fact because I want to make it clear that I am not approaching this subject from any narrow, partisan political view, but rather from the point of view that the principles involved here, as far as I am concerned, cut rather deeply into the moral fabric of society.
For that reason, as I say, as far as I am personally concerned, in an instance of this kind the onus should be put upon the company to prove beyond any peradventure of doubt that this stock split is necessary to the continued financial health of their operation before I would be prepared to go along with the principle of this bill. That is one of the reasons I feel that the amendment we now have before us is proper.
I hope that serious consideration will be given by other hon. members to the desirability of following this course in the case we now have before us. I was interested enough to look at the debates that took place when the bill to incorporate this company was first introduced into the house, and to note some of the assurances that were given to the house at that time by the then hon. member for Vancouver South, Mr. Arthur Laing. One of the assurances he gave was that this was going to be a company which would bring oil to the coast of British Columbia and, as I understood him to present the matter to the house at that time, that it
Private Bills
would be used only for the development of the oil extraction industry in British Columbia.
I think most of us in British Columbia recognize the fact that British Columbia at the present time at least may not be able to absorb the full capacity of that line. Nevertheless we had a right to expect that the line would be used for the development of the oil processing industry in British Columbia, and that the products surplus to our needs would go into adjacent markets after having been processed in British Columbia. I think one must have that consideration in mind when one considers the request that is now before the house with respect to this stock split.
I believe one must analyse the record of the company to date. One must realize that while the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company as such is engaged in the transportation of oil, nevertheless it is in fact a tool-and I am not using that word in any derogatory sense-of certain producing and manufacturing oil companies of this country and of the United States, and that therefore its actions cannot be considered only in the light of the operations of an independent company. Because of that fact we must realize that the policies which they have followed, and which have been dictated to them as a corporate entity by those who control them, must affect our attitude to the application they now have before parliament.
I know this is perhaps a matter of more interest to those of us who live in British Columbia than it is to those who may live in other parts of the country. Nevertheless I think the principle involved should concern members from all parts of the country. I hope recognition will be given to the fact that the economic situation in British Columbia is as important to those of us who live there as is the economic situation in the region of Canada around which discussion revolved in a recent debate in this house.
I hope other hon. members will take advantage of the opportunity to express their views on the principle of the bill, and in particular upon the amendment which has just been moved and which, as I have suggested, should go a long way toward meeting some of the objections which were raised when the bill was first up for debate in the house.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on behalf of my colleague the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., who is unable to be here today and who is the sponsor of this bill. 1 am not going to get into any prolonged discussion of the rather remarkable amendment moved by

my good friend the hon. member for Nanaimo, because it seemed to me that by the nature of the amendment he moved he gave away his own case. I am certainly not going to get into any involved argument as to whether or not you can submit the subject matter of a very complicated thing like this to a committee without submitting the reason for the discussion in the first place. I shall just content myself by saying that even if we were to vote for the amendment, the only result of that vote would be to accomplish by a very inefficient, confused and involved way what we are asked to do in the bill itself.
Without making any comment whatever on the merits of this bill, I should say it is a very simple submission to this house. We are simply asked to give to this company, a very prosperous British Columbia company of which a great many of us, contrary to some of my friends opposite, are quite proud, the opportunity to do business in the same way a great many other companies do. We are quite proud of the fact that this company, after overcoming the original difficulties it faced, has managed to do so well in the matter of a very few years. I for one believe it is most vexatious and irresponsible for anyone in this house to stand up and say that any company should not have the right to do what all its competitors in the same field are doing.
But ignoring all that, surely there is a very special way for us to deal with all these very real, complicated questions. Surely the way is for us to not continue wasting time, the very limited time we have in these private members' hours. We must be able to find out all the complicated facts about the financing of this company we are discussing. We have to get this before a committee, and the whole purpose of this bill is to get the matter before the appropriate committee of this house.
Therefore, just referring back to the original debates of this house, I recall that my very distinguished predecessor, the hon. member for Vancouver South at that time, had the great honour of being the sponsor of the original bill. I see that at that time there were some submissions made by the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra which concerned the route of the pipe line.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I think I should say one word about my good friend the hon. member for Nanaimo. I think the one thing that distinguishes my own thinking from his thinking is that he seems to resent the fact we have private corporations in this country that are making a good profit. It is on that point I cannot go along with him.

I would be extremely pleased to have a profitable company in my riding. I was astonished the other day when I heard the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam almost bemoaning the fact that this company, which is located in his riding, has been showing a good profit for the last couple of years. I will tell him that if he does not want corporations in his constituency making a good profit, I shall be glad to have them move into Vancouver South.
Speaking very seriously, how in the name of common sense are we going to continue to raise the money we require in this country to finance family allowances and old age pensions, especially with the more generous old age pension that some of us believe is necessary, unless we have prosperous companies operating in this country? I for one am extremely glad we have a prosperous oil company operating in British Columbia. I know of no reason why this company should not be treated in the same manner as all the other private businesses operating in western Canada. I think this house should approve the bill and send it to the appropriate committee, where my hon. friends opposite will have unlimited time to crossexamine the officials of the company. Then they can deal with facts, and not have to continue dealing with fiction.

Mr. Speaker, there is one point which I think should be kept clear, and I realize it is a point upon which the house frequently gets confused. There is no question but that a private bill such as the bill that has been introduced by the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., if it is given second reading, has to go to the committee. We know that; all hon. members of the house know that. But, Mr. Speaker-and I recall your interest in this
Private Bills
point in the days before you were exalted to your present position-there is a difference in our view between sending to a committee a bill which has been given second reading, and sending to a committee the subject matter of a bill.
If we had before us merely the motion for second reading and that motion were to pass, of course the bill would go to the committee; but it would go as having had the endorsement of its principle by this house. We do not think this bill should have its principle endorsed before it goes to the committee. That is the reason for the amendment that has been moved by my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo. We are quite prepared to have the subject matter of this bill discussed by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. We are also quite prepared to have the promoters of this bill go before that committee and state their reasons why parliament should consider this bill. But from our study of its provisions we feel that that questioning and discussion should take place in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines before the House of Commons has been asked to endorse the principle of this bill. That is the reason for our amendment.
I say again, either way the matter will be referred to the committee. If the bill passes second reading the bill itself goes to the committee. If the present amendment passes, instead of the bill going to the committee the subject matter will go before it, and discussion will take place on the subject matter without the House of Commons having endorsed the principle of the bill.
I want to join with my colleagues the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, the hon. member for Nanaimo and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, who have already spoken, in saying that we feel this bill should not be supported.
